q: Student motivation begins with the internal work of teaching. We can decry the obstacles to student motivation today — kids' tendency to either care too much about grades or to not care about them at all; our students' access to exponentially more entertainment than ever before in world history — but there aren't many good excuses for harboring poor, negative, self-fulfilling beliefs in ourselves. Our insides are the most fertile ground we till.
If you're certain that you're a bad teacher, then you're probably right. At the very least, you're on your way there. I feel bad saying it so directly, but here's the thing: beliefs drive behavior.

When we pigeonhole kids, they perceive it, and they're likely to act accordingly. We all — kids and teachers — act in ways that mesh with who we are. Daphna Oyserman calls this “identity-congruent behavior.

If you're certain that what you're teaching is pointless, then it probably will be for most of your kids. Professionals take what they're required to teach and they creatively seek to make it worthwhile for their students.

And they trust me more, too, because they know that A) I tell them the truth, and B) I put my money where my mouth is when it comes to doing hard things. Just because I don't like the book doesn't mean I don't teach kids to read and analyze and discuss it for all I'm worth.)

You're not right because of any objective reality — after all, Jacie's motivation is rooted in her beliefs, and her beliefs are malleable — but rather, you're right because the way that you're thinking about Jacie ensures that you won't try much to get her on board with her education.
x: Dave Stuart Jr. argues that student motivation begins with the internal work of teaching, because the negative beliefs teachers hold about themselves, their students and their content tend to become self-fulfilling.
Teachers' beliefs are self-fulfilling: a teacher certain they are bad, or that content is pointless, is on the way to being right.
Beliefs drive behavior for teachers just as they do for kids.
Teachers should creatively make required content worthwhile and not expect students to value a lesson the teacher does not.
Beliefs drive behavior for teachers just as they do for kids.
Writing off a student like Jacie guarantees failure not because of any objective reality but because the teacher stops trying.

t: The Most Effective Way To Manage Students With ADHD
q: It's to be great at classroom management. It's to double-down on the approach we recommend here at SCM.
Because this will always have the greatest impact on students with ADHD—their improvement, contentment, and ability to focus and really enjoy school. It’s not even close.
You see, no other strategy, including those I’m going to recommend as part of a future e-guide, will have much effect until and unless the first is accomplished.
But when placed in the right environment, many will quietly assimilate into the calm and well-behaved culture just like everyone else—and without extra attention from the teacher.
There is an epidemic of students who are misunderstood, labeled, pigeonholed, over-managed, and in some cases, even misdiagnosed due to poor classroom management.
But it isn’t worth much unless you create the conditions through which all students can overcome their behavioral and academic challenges.
x: No other ADHD-specific strategy will be effective until strong baseline classroom management is already in place.
A calm, distraction-free environment has an outsized impact on students struggling with restlessness and impulsivity.

t: The Five Questions Our Students Are Asking, All the Time
q: All of our students, throughout the school year and especially at the start, are asking five questions. The level of motivation they'll bring to their work in our rooms isn't set in stone on Day One, or on Day 100.
Teacher credibility has one of the highest effect sizes in John Hattie's Visible Learning meta-analysis. Here are some ways to build it, and here are some ways to undermine it.
Teaching is a cool job because we get to experiment with Value cultivation every day. And our kids are required by law to come to our class and be our guinea pigs.

Hard work is hard, so us human beings typically need to believe it's going to pay off if we're going to do it in the first place. If I just believe that, no matter what, I'll never do 100 push-ups, then guess what? I probably won't do a single push-up today.

I've been talking with some of my students lately who are certain of the fact that they're going to transfer to the alternative high school as soon as they rack up enough failed classes. When I ask them why they're so bent on this, they say, “I can't learn in this high school.” This is the Efficacy belief's opposite: I'm sure that I will fail.
Students' sense of their belonging in our classes and schools can be affected by anything from sharing a birthday with someone else to experiencing moments of genuine connection with you.
x: Student motivation is a moving target shaped by five recurring, mostly unconscious questions, so teachers must keep answering them all year rather than only in the first week.
He notes that teacher credibility carries one of the highest effect sizes in Hattie's work and that beliefs, not laziness, drive behavior.
Efficacy is complicated because students define success differently, from passing with a D- to needing a 93%, so teachers must help kids define success.

Each question maps to one of his key beliefs: Credibility (do I have a good teacher), Value (does this work matter), Effort (will my effort pay off), Efficacy (can I succeed), and Belonging (do people like me belong here).
Efficacy is complicated because students define success differently, from passing with a D- to needing a 93%, so teachers must help kids define success.
Belonging can be shifted by something as small as a shared birthday or a moment of genuine connection with the teacher.

t: Why Your Humor Isn't Working In Your Classroom
q: If you care too much and overthink it, you’ll lose your spontaneity. You’ll lose your timing and playfulness, your cleverness and quirkiness.
A classroom is a target-rich environment and by simply being aware and open-minded, what to say or do at the right moment will come to you without conscious thought.
But even professional comedians have to spend months, sometimes years, on their material, working out the perfect timing, pacing, and word choice just to get a reliable laugh.
When you try to be cool or speak to students on their level, using their lingo, attitudes, or sensibilities, it never works.
One of the tenets of improvisational comedy, which is the true secret to bringing more humor to your classroom, is to not try to be funny.
Just focus on enjoying your students and the laughs, the easy rapport, the likability, the love of being in your class . . . Will happen naturally.
x: Trying too hard to be funny undermines spontaneity, timing, and authentic personality.
Linsin addresses teachers who feel their attempts at humor fall flat, arguing the problem isn't a lack of natural wit but three common mistakes.
Planning or rehearsing jokes rarely works in the classroom, since even professional comedians need extensive practice to appear natural.
Attempting to be "cool" or relatable by adopting student slang or attitudes reads as inauthentic and damages rapport.
The core fix, borrowed from improvisational comedy, is to stop trying to be funny and instead stay present and authentically oneself.
He closes by urging teachers to focus on enjoying their students rather than pursuing laughs directly.

t: How I Prove to My Students that They Actually Can Memorize Things
q: Knowing things — rather than being able to Google things — facilitates further knowledge-building, critical thinking, and literacy. There are many ways we can come to know things — incidental learning, topic immersion, inquiry, and so on — and one of those ways is just straight-up memorization.

Near the start of the school year before I give my kids their first list like this, I have them write a 100-word quickwrite warm-up on the following prompt: Are you the kind of person who can memorize a list of dates? How do you know? What kinds of things in your life do you memorize, and how do you do that?

Step Two: Cover up your list, and now write that list of dates from memory. (I black out the projector at this point.) Write down every scrap that you can remember — every bit of numbers, every bit of event description. It's okay to be wrong — get as much down as you can. (I give 1-2 minutes here.)
And then, I want you to make List 2 perfect, just like List 1. Cross things out, erase, use arrows, but make List 2 perfect.

Step Five: Okay. Get out Lists 1 and 2 and use them to correct List 3. Again, give yourself a score, and again, make List 3 perfect, like Lists 1 and 2. How many people improved their score from List 2 to List 3? (At this point, almost all hands go up.)
Memorization isn't our “thing” — long-term flourishing is — but it's one activity we'll come back to repeatedly to strengthen our minds and hearts throughout the year.
It doesn't matter that there's Google — I want it in their brains, and I want to show them that there's a lot of under-advertised joy in this old-fashioned idea of building knowledge.
x: Dave Stuart Jr. argues that memorization still matters in the age of Google because knowing things facilitates further knowledge-building, critical thinking and literacy.
The activity uses a five-item list and four write-from-memory cycles with self-scoring, so nearly every student visibly improves from List 2 to List 3.

t: A Simple Way To Build Rapport With Challenging Students
q: There is a strategy that builds strong, behavior-influencing rapport with virtually any student.
It’s about your genuine desire to get to know them, nothing more.
But you must have no ulterior motive, no hidden agenda, no strings attached. Because if you do, if you think of it as a strategy to get something from them, they’ll know it.
Be direct and refrain from using praise or flattery to try to get them to open up. This is a common tactic that communicates loud and clear that you do, in fact, have an ulterior motive.
In time, you’ll discover common interests and be drawn into wanting to learn more and more about them. Inevitably, they’ll also become curious about you.
x: Genuine, unconditional interest in a student as a person—without any hidden agenda—builds rapport even with the most guarded students.

Linsin describes a strategy that builds behavior-influencing rapport with even the most guarded or difficult students: taking a genuine, unconditional interest in them as people, with no hidden agenda or expected outcome.
Students can detect an ulterior motive behind adult curiosity and will shut down further if they sense one.
Students can detect an ulterior motive behind adult curiosity and will shut down further if they sense one.
The law of reciprocity eventually causes students to become curious about the teacher and more engaged with the rest of the class.

t: I Stopped Holding My Students Accountable And Here Is What Happened d-heres-what-happened/
q: For one week, I decided to no longer rely on my classroom management plan. That's right. I just stopped following it.
By Wednesday morning, it was clear that their opinion of me had dropped a few notches.
My leverage and influence was fading before my eyes and my leadership presence was fading before theirs.

One thing I found especially interesting about the experiment, and heartening, frankly, was that as the week went on more and more students approached me to ask variations of, “What are you doing?” “Why are you doing this?” and “Are you okay?
Done right, as we recommend here at SCM, accountability is a powerful force for good. It’s a wonderful benefit for students and indispensable to creating a happy and well-behaved class.
x: Linsin recounts a personal experiment: for one week, midway through a semester with a well-behaved class, he deliberately stopped enforcing his classroom management plan while keeping his personality and demeanor unchanged.

Linsin recounts a personal experiment: for one week, midway through a semester with a well-behaved class, he deliberately stopped enforcing his classroom management plan while keeping his personality and demeanor unchanged.
By the end of the week he felt his influence and leadership presence fading despite ramped-up friendliness, while several students began anxiously asking if something was wrong with him.
A week-long experiment removing consequences, while keeping demeanor unchanged, caused measurable deterioration in student relationships.
Kindness and good humor alone proved insufficient to sustain a well-behaved class without accountability as a counterpart.

t: Humble-Boldness: A Common Trait of the Greatest Teachers
q: To be good at teaching, you need to do a few things well, getting better at them as your career progresses. And then you need to do all the rest of the things just well enough.
Greatness at teaching is the fruit of consistent, wisely applied effort over the long-term. Helping you and me become great is why I write this blog.

On the one hand, we need to be humble enough to realize that we're not omnipotent in the classroom — none of this “I'm not going to let you fail” stuff. We're professionals, not saviors. Humble people rightly sense that they are not the center of the cosmos; they don't try to be in the middle of their students' lives.

Sometimes people confuse self-pity for humility. They're not the same. When we fail at reaching a certain kid or the unit assessment scores come back badly, a humble person doesn't sit there grousing about how bad they are at teaching.
To be humble is to live as if you are a servant. A servant's life is about the person served. The good servant is devoid of self-obsession — he doesn't pity himself or pride himself.

As insane as it is, expansive studies show that student life trajectories can be shifted in brief, less-than-60-minute lessons. The classroom contexts we create matter. Simple moments of genuine connection can be transformative.

On the one hand, when things go poorly despite our best efforts, we can say, “Well, that makes sense — I'm only a servant.” We don't take it personally or get internally destroyed. And on the other hand, we don't give up after a hard day because we know how much long-term flourishing potential lies in every lesson and interaction.
x: Good teaching means doing a few important things well and satisficing the rest, while greatness is the fruit of staying at it for years.

Stuart argues that great teaching comes from sustained, wisely applied effort over many years, and that sticking to the work requires a paired disposition he calls humble-boldness, borrowed from Tim Keller.
Humility means recognizing that we are professionals, not saviors, and that the classroom does not revolve around us.
Humility in teaching means being a servant rather than a savior, and it is distinct from self-pity, which is another form of pride.
Humility in teaching means being a servant rather than a savior, and it is distinct from self-pity, which is another form of pride.
Boldness comes from evidence that brief lessons and simple moments of genuine connection can shift student life trajectories, so our efforts carry real significance.
Holding both traits keeps teachers from being destroyed by failure and from quitting after hard days, which is what long-term persistence requires.
